title: Establish Accounts: Email Accounts
summary: Email accounts are the hinge of persona work, because almost every other service, including domain registration, cloud tenancy, code hosting and trial subscriptions, verifies identity through a mailbox. The adversary therefore creates mailboxes meant to survive scrutiny: mainstream providers when a plausible corporate identity is needed, disposable services when anonymity matters more, and addresses shaped to resemble a person or a brand. Reputation filters score sending history, so the mailbox is often used for harmless traffic first. The parent technique covers accounts of any kind, while this sub-technique is specifically about mailboxes and the access they unlock. Detection leans on registration metadata, sending patterns, domain age and authentication results rather than message wording alone.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker creates email accounts to use as tools. Email is needed to sign up for almost every other service, so it usually comes first. The account may look like a person or like a company. Some attackers use free providers, and some use services that hide who they are. The parent idea covers all kinds of accounts, but this part is only about mailboxes.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most online services confirm who you are by sending a message to your email. Whoever owns the mailbox can create and control those other accounts. A mailbox that sends a few normal messages first can later pass simple spam filters. Attackers also use mailboxes to receive replies from people they are tricking. If your staff reply to a fake address, the conversation moves somewhere your security tools may not watch. Blocking one address is easy, but the attacker can make another.
howItWorks: The attacker signs up with an email provider, sometimes one that hides their identity.
They choose an address that looks like a person or a real company.
They warm up the mailbox by sending harmless messages and collecting a few friendly replies.
They use the mailbox to register domains, cloud storage and other services.
They then send phishing messages or join threads that other people started.
If the account is blocked, they move to the next mailbox at almost no cost.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat where the front door intercom is linked to one phone. Whoever holds that phone decides who gets let in. The flat has many rooms and many services, but only one buzzer. An email address works the same way. It opens the door to cloud storage, domains and social accounts, because every service checks the buzzer before letting anyone in. Create or steal the buzzer and the whole building becomes easier to reach.
takeaways: Email is close to a master key for most other online services.
Treat unexpected changes to mailbox rules and recovery settings as serious.
Check the full sending address, not only the display name.

objectives: Explain why email accounts are needed to acquire other infrastructure.
Distinguish this sub-technique from the wider account establishment technique.
Identify mailbox signals that indicate a recently built persona.
Describe how a mailbox is used to send phishing or collect replies.
Recommend checks on mailbox rules and recovery settings.
